Chapter Six: Navigating Resistance and Overcoming Setbacks
No matter how strong your intentions are, or how committed you are to your daily practice, resistance is just part of the journey when you’re building new habits. It can sneak in as procrastination, self-doubt, or even that urge to slip right back into old routines—especially when life gets hectic or stressful. But here’s the thing: instead of viewing resistance as a sign you’ve failed, what if you saw it as a gentle nudge? It’s really just your mind’s way of telling you to pause, pay attention, and maybe tweak your approach.
The first step in understanding resistance is simple—get curious about it. Rather than pushing back or feeling bad about yourself, just take a breath and ask, “What’s really happening here?” Sometimes, resistance pops up because there’s fear—maybe you’re worried about change, about feeling uncomfortable, or about not meeting your own expectations. Other times, it’s just your brain looking for the path of least resistance, sticking to what’s familiar.
So, how can you actually work with resistance instead of against it? Here are a few down-to-earth strategies:
First, give your resistance a name. Maybe it’s “the inner critic,” or “the comfort-seeker.” By labeling it, you make it less intimidating and a lot easier to handle.
Next, ask yourself what that resistance is trying to protect you from or help you avoid. Often, it just wants to keep things safe and predictable.
And finally, respond with compassion. Treat your resistance like a part of yourself that just needs a little understanding—not judgment.
For example, let’s say you’re trying to start a new morning routine, but you keep hitting the snooze button again and again. Instead of beating yourself up, you could simply notice, “Hey, I’m feeling tired and not very motivated this morning.” Then, gently ask what might help—maybe you need to get to bed a little earlier, or make your morning a bit more enjoyable.
Now, let’s talk about setbacks—because they’re bound to happen. Missing a day, slipping back into old habits, or getting thrown off by something unexpected doesn’t wipe out all your progress. What really matters is how you respond when setbacks show up. That all-or-nothing thinking—like believing one misstep means you’ve totally failed—can make it even harder to bounce back. Instead, try to see setbacks as opportunities to learn and adjust.
Here are some ways to get back on track after a setback:
First, remind yourself that nobody’s perfect. We all stumble—and that’s completely normal.
Take a moment to reflect. What led to the setback? And what could you try differently next time?
And most importantly, recommit as soon as you can. The quicker you return to your habit, the less power that setback has over you.
Picture this: you’ve been eating healthy, but then you find yourself having an unexpected treat at a party. Instead of giving up on your goals, you pause, ask what triggered that choice, forgive yourself, and simply get back to your healthy routine at your next meal.
By meeting resistance and setbacks with curiosity and self-compassion, you can move through the ups and downs of habit change without losing sight of what really matters. Every challenge is a chance to build resilience and deepen your commitment to the journey.
